source.title: Feature-Selective Representation Misdirection for Machine Unlearning
source.authors: Taozhao Chen; Ling-Han Huang; Kim-Kwang Raymond Choo; Hua-Min Chen

record.file_problem: None; the full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: Reports WMDP forgetting and MMLU utility outcomes for unlearning methods, including results across retain-set regimes. It does not test whether attacks recover the knowledge.
record.gate_note: The paper reports unlearning outcomes, not post-unlearning recovery attacks. It gives no chance-level reference for WMDP. Results for LLMU, SCRUB, and SSD in Table 2 are cited from prior work and are not included as rows. Table 4's ablations vary components of the authors' proposed method; they do not test recovery after unlearning, so they are not included.
record.test_reason: The study reproduces RMU and Adaptive RMU and adds SRMU on Zephyr-7B. It reports WMDP forget accuracy and MMLU utility in the standard WikiText-retain setting and in a new high-entanglement setting with a same-domain retain set. This bears on the forgetting/utility half of A. No recovery attack of any kind is run, so B–E are not tested, and SRMU is never tested for attack resistance (F).
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that SRMU matches or beats RMU and Adaptive RMU on the forgetting–utility trade-off in the standard setting. They also say it remains more effective under high entanglement, where prior perturbation methods fail for structural rather than tuning reasons. Their ablations show both the importance map and the directional vector are needed.
record.recipe_differences: SRMU is a new feature-aware representation-editing objective using an importance map and directional misdirection vector; RMU and Adaptive RMU are reproduced as comparators. This paper does not apply recovery attacks.
record.method_sensitivity: Retain-set regime changes outcomes: results differ between WikiText low-entanglement retention and same-domain high-entanglement retention.
record.problems: No uncertainty estimates are reported. No chance-level reference is given for WMDP, and no recovery attack is evaluated. Table 2's LLMU, SCRUB, and SSD values are cited from prior work rather than reproduced here.
record.rows_left_out: None of the eligible reported results were omitted. Table 4 component ablations were left out because they do not test post-unlearning recovery; cited LLMU, SCRUB, and SSD results in Table 2 were excluded as prior-work results.

untested.parts: Whether simple attacks recover the knowledge. Only post-unlearning benchmark accuracy is measured.
All of it; no relearning or fine-tuning attack.
All of it; no direction ablation or analysis of blocking vs deletion.
All of it; no rephrasing, jailbreak, multilingual or in-context probes.
SRMU's claimed robustness concerns retain-set entanglement only, not resistance to recovery attacks.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's 'V1' tags are invalid and are remapped to A. The chance level (25%, 4-option multiple choice) comes from the WMDP benchmark, not from this paper; the low-entanglement rows are judged near chance on that basis. Results come from a single model (Zephyr-7B) with no uncertainty estimates. LLMU, SCRUB and SSD values are cited from prior work and correctly excluded. In Table 4 the ablation baseline numbers differ slightly from Table 2 (RMU WMDP average 0.2896 vs 28.4). The paper has no recovery attacks, so its evidence bears only on the non-adversarial half of A.

versions.untested_parts: Tests WMDP forgetting and MMLU utility, but not whether simple attacks recover knowledge. A chance-level reference is not stated, so whether WMDP accuracy is near chance cannot be determined.
No fine-tuning or relearning attack is tested.
No activation-direction ablation to recover knowledge is tested, and the paper does not test whether unlearning blocks access rather than deletes knowledge.
No prompt rephrasing, jailbreak, language variation, or in-context recovery attack is tested.
SRMU is evaluated under retain-set entanglement, not for resistance to the attacks in versions B–E.

relation.reason: It reports WMDP and MMLU after RMU and Adaptive RMU in two retain regimes, which bears on the forgetting/utility part of A. It runs no recovery attacks.

tranche.reason: The study proposes a new method (SRMU), so T2 could be argued. It also tests RMU and Adaptive RMU in a new high-entanglement retain setting with a result on A, so T3 holds.

source_check.notes: The authors reproduced RMU and Adaptive RMU and report the best of a [1,170] coefficient sweep. LLMU, SCRUB and SSD are cited from prior work. The paper states no chance level and runs no attack, so only the forgetting/utility part of A is tested. Table 4 gives RMU WMDP avg 0.2896, against 28.4 in Table 2.

statements.correction: This study: Zephyr-7B, WikiText retain set, authors' best-of-sweep RMU reproduction. WMDP avg 54.7->28.4 (Bio 64.7->28.8, Cyber 44.8->28.0), MMLU 58.5->56.9. Unlearn layer not reported. No attack run. Same-domain retain set: WMDP avg 44.8.
statements.problem: No number is attributed to this study by name. The cited rows R01/R04 fit the 24-29% and 0-4-pt ranges. The 3-10 layer range and the other models come from other studies, and 'why' leaves this study out.

statements.correction: Zephyr-7B, same-domain retain set: WMDP avg 54.7->44.8 (RMU) and 43.54 (Adaptive RMU), MMLU 58.5->51.9 and 51.15. WikiText retain set: Adaptive RMU 26.0, SRMU 27.2, RMU 28.4. Authors say sweeps show the high-entanglement limit is not tuning.
Zephyr-7B, WikiText retain set: WMDP avg 26.0-28.4 for RMU, Adaptive RMU and SRMU. Same-domain retain set: RMU 44.8, Adaptive RMU 43.54 (MMLU 51.9, 51.15; base 58.5). SRMU there: 37.7, MMLU 52.5.
